about: Mabel's annotations, an invented case. Every participant turn in order, found by its opening words: its experiential statements and each one's key quote, quote and statement in the same order, a gap in a quote marked with an ellipsis, its exploratory note and the words highlighted, or empty for a turn reviewed and left empty. Then the times of the work and her PET board. make_demo.py builds the workbook, the progress file and the themes file from this and the interview CSV beside it.

turns.at: Well. It's noisy, for a start.
es: A dog like having the lights on
turns.en: Her image is light, not noise, though the noise comes first as a joke. Before, a cup still there in the morning.
kq: It's like having the lights on. That's the nearest I can get to it.
turns.crux: It's like having the lights on.

turns.at: No. And I'm a tidy person, or I was.
es: Glad of the mess: after two still years, signs of life in the house
turns.en: Two years of stillness, named plainly. The glasses case in the dog's bed counts as evidence of life.
kq: So it's a funny thing to be glad of. But a house where things stay put is a house where nothing's happening. I had two years of that and I don't want it back. … It means somebody's been living here.

turns.at: She gets me up at seven.
es: Up at seven for the dog, where before there was nothing to get up for
turns.en: The days before had no start. A polite insistence, felt through the eyelids. New clothes for a new routine.
kq: Before her I'd lie there till nine some days, there wasn't anything to get up for. … Now it's seven o'clock, dressing gown, kettle on, let her out, and we're on the green by half past. Rain or shine.

es: Through the dog, a morning society she never knew was there
turns.en: A world there all along, opened to her with the dog. She knows its etiquette and explains it.
kq: Oh, it's a whole society. You wouldn't know it unless you had a dog. … I'd lived on this estate twenty years and I didn't know them.

turns.at: It's lovely. I don't want to overdo it
es: Back among people without having to try, after losing the habit
turns.en: No effort asked of her, the dog is the reason to be there. Help given as well as taken.
kq: It's lovely. I don't want to overdo it, but it's saved me a bit. … I'd lost the habit. You forget how. And with a dog you don't need to know how … the talking just happens round the edges.
turns.crux: the talking just happens round the edges

es: With the dog depending on her, eating properly again after a bad winter
turns.en: She plays down her own word, saved. Feeding the dog and feeding herself go together in her telling.
kq: But I was in a bad way that second winter on my own. … And now I've got to be up and out and someone's depending on me, and you can't feed a dog and not feed yourself, it looks ridiculous. So I eat. I sit down to it.

es: Six months of thinking the dog a terrible mistake
turns.en: Doubt at the start, told with humour. The fall comes quickly, almost comic.
kq: No. Oh, no. The first six months I thought I'd made a terrible mistake.

es: Her daughter's care felt as being treated like a child
turns.en: She grants her daughter's care and still feels something taken from her.
kq: She thought she was looking after me, and she was, I know she was. But it felt like she was taking something off me. Like I was a child who'd been given a puppy and couldn't be trusted with it.

es: Feeling small, and frightened for herself and the dog
Sure by morning she was keeping the dog
turns.en: The night in the sling, two fears side by side. The decision is there by morning, without argument.
kq: I felt small. And frightened too, if I'm honest, because she had a point, hadn't she. … what if it had been my hip. What happens to her then. What happens to me.
I didn't sleep much. But I knew I wasn't giving her up. I knew that by the morning.

es: Learning patience with the dog at seventy three, and it paying off, mostly
turns.en: At my age: pride as much as surprise. Patience as her answer to the fall.
kq: I took her to classes. At my age! … It takes forever. The first week it took us forty minutes to get to the end of the road. But she learned. She walks nicely now, mostly.

turns.at: Better. She came to watch a class
es: Peace with her daughter, unspoken, shown in a chew
turns.en: Mending without talking about it. She finds it in the chew.
kq: We've not talked about it since, really. But she brings Pepper a chew when she comes now. That's how I know.

turns.at: All the time. Not in a gloomy way.
es: Providing for a dog likely to outlive her, practical more than gloomy
turns.en: The losing turned round: her own death and the dog's future. Responsible, she says, not morbid.
kq: Not in a gloomy way. Well, sometimes in a gloomy way. But mostly practical. … She could well outlive me. So I've sorted it. … My daughter thought that was morbid. I think it's the most responsible thing I've ever done.

turns.at: Strange. Sitting in the solicitor's office
es: Lighter once the dog's future was settled
turns.en: The will sets the dog among Dennis's things and the house. Relief in the body, on the wall outside.
kq: But I came out and sat on the wall outside and I felt lighter. Like I'd put something down. Because it had been sitting with me, the not knowing, every time she looked at me.

turns.at: Yes. Because she does, you see.
es: Unable to bear the thought of the dog waiting and her never coming
turns.en: Waiting is the image that carries it. Her own death matters here as the dog's loss.
kq: When I go to the shops she's at the window when I come back. Every time. … And I couldn't bear the thought of her doing that and me never coming.

es: Telling the dog her day, as she once told Dennis
turns.en: The habit of a marriage finds a listener. She laughs at herself and keeps on.
kq: And sometimes I catch myself and think, Mabel, you're telling a dog the price of butter. But it's a habit of forty years, telling someone about your day. It had nowhere to go. Now it goes to her.

es: Glad of the dog's breathing in the night, on his side of the bed
turns.en: She closes the subject herself, I'll say that and leave it there. The side of the bed is his.
kq: She's on the bed now. On his side. … But it's nice to hear breathing. I'll say that and leave it there. It's nice to hear breathing in the night again.

turns.at: Only that I didn't expect it.
es: Opened out of a shut-in life by the dog, and mostly glad
turns.en: Her own summary, sleet and all. Glad, said twice.
kq: Only that I didn't expect it. Any of it. … She opened the door, really, that's what it is. I was shut in and she opened the door. Some mornings I'd still rather she hadn't, when it's sleeting. But mostly I'm glad.
